Olyka Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Olyka, Ukraine

Demolished. This cemetery appears on mid-19th-century Russian maps, presumably established in the 18th century; on July 3, 1941, some Olyka Jews were shot here, and the site was later demolished by Nazi occupiers, who used its tombstones for town-center road construction. Residents recall remnants still present as late as 1966, before final demolition under Soviet rule in 1967. About 0.5 hectares of the site, along with a recently recovered matzevah fragment, are reportedly earmarked by Jewish community representatives for a memorial chapel (presumably an ohel), though no contact with them was established. Jews settled in Olyka in the mid-16th century, first mentioned in 1577; many survived the 1648 Khmelnytsky uprising by hiding in the local fortress. The 17th-century community, one of Volyn's largest, gained independence; early-18th-century fires reduced the population by 75% to 547, recovering to 2,606 (62%) by 1897. Two synagogues and the cemetery existed by 1847; the Hirsh Leib Landau Hasidic dynasty was founded in Olyka, and nine synagogues plus a Jewish hospital operated by the early 20th century. WWI brought Cossack attacks, Russian invasion, and gang pillaging; many Jews joined Zionist organizations after 1917. Population reached 2,086 by 1921, the same period a Jewish cooperative bank and Hebrew school opened, followed by a 1920s-30s yeshiva department. Population reached about 2,500 by 1941. Wehrmacht occupation from June 27, 1941 established a ghetto on March 13, 1942, absorbing outlying Jews, liquidated in late July 1942; 5,220 Jews were murdered in the Olyka region during occupation. Three monuments mark mass-shooting sites, installed in 1967, 1990, and 2005.
